Self-esteem and identity

Self-compassion: treating yourself like a good friend

Being hard on yourself does not usually motivate you more. Being kind to yourself after mistakes helps you improve.

When a friend makes a mistake, we tend to say something like "it could happen to anyone, you'll sort it out". When we make one ourselves, we often speak to ourselves with a harshness we would never use with anyone else.

What self-compassion is

The psychologist Kristin Neff defined it in 2003 with three components: kindness towards yourself rather than harsh criticism; recognising that making mistakes and suffering are part of a shared human experience, rather than feeling you are the only one; and mindfulness to acknowledge distress without exaggerating or ignoring it.

It is not the same as self-esteem or as settling for less. Many people fear that being kind to themselves will make them lazy. But in a 2012 study, Juliana Breines and Serena Chen found that people encouraged to be self-compassionate after a failure studied more to improve on a later test and were more willing to make amends for a moral lapse. A meta-analysis that same year linked more self-compassion with less anxiety and depression.

It is not self-indulgence

A common fear is that being kind to yourself leads to complacency. Studies say otherwise. In an experiment by Juliana Breines and Serena Chen, students encouraged to think self-compassionately about an exam that had gone badly studied longer for the next one than those who only received self-esteem boosting messages. Being understanding about one's mistakes makes it easier to face them and correct them.

Self-compassion and health

A 2012 meta-analysis found a strong association between self-compassion and fewer symptoms of anxiety, depression and stress. There are training programmes, such as Kristin Neff and Christopher Germer's Mindful Self-Compassion, with favourable trials. A simple exercise in a difficult moment is to put a hand on your chest and say something like: "This is hard. Everyone goes through this sometimes. What do I need right now?"

What usually helps

  • Notice how you talk to yourself. If you would not say it to a friend, perhaps you should not say it to yourself either.
  • Remember you are not the only one. Many people go through the same thing.
  • Separate the behaviour from the person: "I did something wrong" is not the same as "I'm a disaster".
  • Ask yourself what you need right now: rest, help or a plan for the next step.

References

  1. Neff, K. D. (2003). Self-compassion: an alternative conceptualization of a healthy attitude toward oneself. Self and Identity, 2(2), 85–101.
  2. Breines, J. G. y Chen, S. (2012). Self-compassion increases self-improvement motivation. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 38(9), 1133–1143.
  3. MacBeth, A. y Gumley, A. (2012). Exploring compassion: a meta-analysis of the association between self-compassion and psychopathology. Clinical Psychology Review, 32(6), 545–552.
